title: The Marauder’s Map: Bézier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Biological systems adapt through small, localized structural changes at fine scale, preserving existing function, which motivates flexible degeneracy as a design principle.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed zoom-in from whole neuron to dendrite
description: A black silhouette of a pyramidal neuron, with branching dendrites on top and roots at the bottom, sits on the left. A small purple dashed circle on one dendrite branch connects through dashed purple lines to a large purple dashed box on the right. The box shows a magnified black dendrite segment with a bumpy outline. Three colored annotations mark local changes. Yellow bulb-shaped spines are labeled 'synaptic clustering'. A black dotted outline of a removed spine is labeled 'synapse deletion'. Thin blue protrusions are labeled 'filopodia'. The labels are large and use the same colors as the structures they name. The eye goes first to the magnified dendrite and its colored spines, then to the labels. The figure has no math and very little text.
caption: Local degrees of freedom in biological learning. Dendrites support synaptic clustering (yellow), deletion (dashed), and filopodia (blue) carrying silent synapses that can become active. These localized mechanisms of change let circuits learn without overwriting existing function.
abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional BÃ©zier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.
